Colossians 1.summary: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy greet the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae (Colossians 1:1-2). They always thank God because they have heard of the Colossians' faith in Christ Jesus and their love for all the saints, because of the hope laid up for them in heaven, which they heard in the word of the truth, the gospel (Colossians 1:3-5). The gospel is bearing fruit and increasing in the whole world and among the Colossians, who learned it from Epaphras, a beloved fellow servant and faithful minister of Christ (Colossians 1:6-8). The writers have prayed since they heard, asking that the Colossians be filled with the knowledge of God's will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, bear fruit, increase in the knowledge of God, be strengthened with all power for endurance and patience with joy, and give thanks to the Father, who has qualified them to share in the inheritance of the saints in light (Colossians 1:9-12). God has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins (Colossians 1:13-14). Then comes a great description of Christ: he is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; all things were created by him, through him and for him; he is before all things and in him all things hold together; he is the head of the body, the church, the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him God reconciled to himself all things, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:15-20). The Colossians, once alienated and hostile in mind, have been reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, to be presented holy and blameless, if indeed they continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel (Colossians 1:21-23). Paul rejoices in his sufferings for their sake, and describes his stewardship from God to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages but now revealed to the saints, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:24-27). Paul and his companions proclaim Christ, warning and teaching everyone with all wisdom to present everyone mature in Christ, and for this Paul toils, struggling with all the energy that Christ powerfully works within him (Colossians 1:28-29).
Colossians 1.whereWeAre:
Epaphras, who is from Colossae (4:12), brought the gospel to the Colossians (1:7), and Paul had not visited them (2:1).

Colossae was an old city. Herodotus called it a great city of Phrygia (Histories 7.30) in the fifth century BC, though by the first century its importance had declined relative to nearby Laodicea.

Paul writes from prison, but the location is not stated in the letter. Rome, Caesarea and Ephesus have each been proposed, and the question is disputed.

The letter names several co-workers who are also named in Philemon (Onesimus, Archippus, Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke, Demas), which suggests that the two letters were written at about the same time.

Many Jews lived in Phrygia and Lydia. The Jewish historian Josephus says Josephus preserves a letter in which Antiochus III orders two thousand Jewish families to be moved from Mesopotamia and Babylonia to Lydia and Phrygia (Antiquities 12.147-153). The thanksgiving and prayer show a church that Paul knew only by report, and the hymn to Christ speaks of Christ's supremacy over all things, which fits the concerns Paul takes up in chapter 2. The emphasis on Christ's rule over all powers fits a setting where other powers were being given a role.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Greets the church, gives thanks and prays, and describes his ministry and suffering. His apostleship and stewardship underlie the letter's authority.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Joins in the greeting. Part of the team writing to the church.

keyFigures.name: The saints and faithful brothers at Colossae
keyFigures.role: Receive thanks, prayers, and instruction. The audience of the letter.

keyFigures.name: Epaphras
keyFigures.role: Brought the gospel to them and told Paul of their love in the Spirit. The link between Paul and the church, who had not met Paul.

keyFigures.name: Christ Jesus
keyFigures.role: Creator, sustainer, head of the church, firstborn from the dead, reconciler. The center of the chapter and the letter.

keyFigures.name: God the Father
keyFigures.role: Delivers believers from darkness and reconciles all things through Christ. The source of the gospel.

keyFigures.name: The gentiles (nations)
keyFigures.role: Included in the riches of the glory of the mystery. Shows the inclusion of non-Jews.

keyFigures.name: Thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities
keyFigures.role: Created through and for Christ. Show Christ's rule over all powers.

keyFigures.name: Colossae (place)
keyFigures.role: The city of the recipients. Gives the setting for the letter.

keyThemes.theme: Thanksgiving for faith, hope and love
keyThemes.explanation:
Paul thanks God for the Colossians' faith in Christ, love for all the saints and hope laid up in heaven.

The chapter invites readers to see faith, love and hope together.

keyThemes.theme: Growing in knowledge and fruitful living
keyThemes.explanation:
The prayer asks that they be filled with the knowledge of God's will, walk worthily, bear fruit, and be strengthened.

The passage invites readers to see understanding and action as linked.

Christ is the image of God, Creator, sustainer, head of the church, and firstborn from the dead.

The chapter invites readers to give Christ first place.

God reconciles all things through Christ, making peace by the blood of his cross, and reconciles the Colossians.

The passage invites readers to rest their hope in Christ's death and to continue in the faith.

The mystery hidden for ages, Christ in you, the hope of glory, is made known to all, and Paul toils to present everyone mature in Christ.

Readers are invited to see ministry as proclaiming Christ and aiming at maturity.

Colossians 2.summary: Paul says he has a great struggle for the Colossians, for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen him face to face, that their hearts may be encouraged, knit together in love, and reach full assurance of understanding of God's mystery, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:1-3). He says this so that no one may delude them with plausible arguments, and though absent in body he is with them in spirit, rejoicing in their good order and firm faith (Colossians 2:4-5). As they received Christ Jesus the Lord, so they are to walk in him, rooted, built up and established in the faith, abounding in thanksgiving (Colossians 2:6-7). They are to see to it that no one takes them captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ (Colossians 2:8). In Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and they have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority (Colossians 2:9-10). They were circumcised in him with a circumcision made without hands, buried with him in baptism and raised with him through faith in God's working; God made them alive with him, forgave all their trespasses, canceled the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands, setting it aside, nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the rulers and authorities, putting them to open shame by triumphing over them in him (Colossians 2:11-15). Therefore no one is to pass judgment on them in questions of food and drink, festival, new moon or Sabbath, which are a shadow of things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16-17). No one is to disqualify them by insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up by a sensuous mind and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body grows with a growth that is from God (Colossians 2:18-19). Since they died with Christ to the elemental spirits of the world, they should not submit to regulations such as 'Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch,' which are human precepts and teachings with an appearance of wisdom in self-made religion and severity to the body, but of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh (Colossians 2:20-23).
Colossians 2.whereWeAre:
Jews lived in the Lycus Valley, and the Roman orator Cicero records that gold intended for the Jerusalem temple was seized in Laodicea in 62 BC (Pro Flacco 28), which shows a significant Jewish presence in the area.

The letter mentions philosophy, tradition, observances, asceticism, angels and visions. It does not say whether these belong to one teaching or several, or what their source was.

Paul had not met the Colossians face to face (2:1) and knew of the church from Epaphras (1:7-8; 4:12-13).

Laodicea was a nearby city and recipient of a separate letter (4:16).

Paul's other letters speak of the 'elemental spirits' (Galatians 4:3, 4:9) and of food and special days (Romans 14:1-6), which shows that similar issues arose elsewhere. The warnings fit a church exposed to teachers who proposed additional rules and experiences. By stressing that all fullness is in Christ, Paul counters these without having to describe them in detail.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Describes his struggle for the churches and warns the Colossians. His concern and authority frame the warnings.

keyFigures.name: The Colossians
keyFigures.role: Urged to walk in Christ and not be taken captive. The audience.

keyFigures.name: Those at Laodicea and others who have not seen Paul
keyFigures.role: Included in Paul's struggle. Shows the wider reach of Paul's concern.

keyFigures.name: Christ Jesus
keyFigures.role: Head of all rule and authority; triumphs over rulers and authorities. The center of the argument.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Made alive, forgave, canceled the record of debt and disarmed the powers. The agent of the saving acts in 2:11-15.

keyFigures.name: Those who would delude, take captive, or disqualify
keyFigures.role: Warned against by Paul. The unnamed opponents who prompt the warnings.

keyFigures.name: Rulers and authorities; the 'elemental spirits'
keyFigures.role: The rulers and authorities are disarmed by God in Christ (2:15); the elemental spirits are named alongside human tradition (2:8) and as something believers died to (2:20). Shows what Christ has defeated.

keyFigures.name: Angels
keyFigures.role: Associated with the worship the letter warns about. Part of the teaching being corrected.

keyThemes.explanation:
In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and in him the whole fullness of deity dwells.

The chapter invites readers to look to Christ as complete.

keyThemes.theme: Beware of human tradition and empty deceit
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are warned not to be taken captive by philosophy, tradition or regulations of human origin.

The passage invites readers to test teaching against Christ.

keyThemes.theme: Union with Christ in death and life
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers were circumcised without hands, buried with Christ in baptism, and raised with him through faith.

The chapter invites readers to see their identity in Christ's death and resurrection.

keyThemes.theme: Forgiveness and victory through the cross
keyThemes.explanation:
God forgave all trespasses, canceled the record of debt, and triumphed over the rulers and authorities.

The passage invites confidence in God's forgiveness and victory.

No one is to pass judgment over food, drink and festivals, which are a shadow; the substance belongs to Christ.

Readers are invited to hold fast to Christ the Head and to be cautious about judging others.

Colossians 3.summary: Paul says that since the Colossians have been raised with Christ, they are to seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, and set their minds on things above and not on earthly things (Colossians 3:1-2). They have died, and their life is hidden with Christ in God; when Christ, who is their life, appears, they will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:3-4). They are to put to death what is earthly in them: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire and covetousness, which is idolatry; the wrath of God is coming on account of these, and they once walked in them (Colossians 3:5-7). They must now put away anger, wrath, malice, slander and obscene talk, and not lie to one another, having put off the old self with its practices and put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator (Colossians 3:8-10). In this new self there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all, and in all (Colossians 3:11). As God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, they are to put on compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving each other as the Lord has forgiven them, and above all to put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony (Colossians 3:12-14). The peace of Christ is to rule in their hearts, they are to be thankful, let the word of Christ dwell in them richly, teach and admonish one another, sing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs with thankfulness, and do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him (Colossians 3:15-17). Paul then addresses households: wives are to submit to their husbands as is fitting in the Lord, and husbands are to love their wives and not be harsh (Colossians 3:18-19); children are to obey their parents in everything, and fathers not to provoke their children (Colossians 3:20-21); bondservants are to obey their earthly masters with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord, working heartily as for the Lord, knowing that they will receive the inheritance as their reward, while the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong done, and there is no partiality (Colossians 3:22-25).
Colossians 3.whereWeAre:
The Roman household (familia) included the head, wife, children, slaves and sometimes freed persons and dependents, and household management was a major theme in Greco-Roman moral writing.

Slavery was widespread in the Roman Empire, and slaves had few legal rights; the letter to Philemon concerns the slave Onesimus, who is also mentioned in Colossians 4:9.

Greek writers used 'barbarian' for people who did not speak Greek, and the Greek historian Herodotus describes the Scythians as nomads north of the Black Sea. The terms reflect cultural prejudice that the passage sets aside.

Early Christians sang psalms, hymns and spiritual songs (3:16; compare Ephesians 5:19) and met in homes (4:15).

Similar household instructions appear in Ephesians 5:22-6:9 and 1 Peter 2:18-3:7, and Greek and Roman writers such as Aristotle discussed household roles (Politics 1.2). The household instruction places Christian life in the daily structures of the first century and adds the motive 'in the Lord,' which gives each relationship a new frame.

keyFigures.name: The Colossian believers
keyFigures.role: Told to seek things above, put off the old self, put on the new self, and live out their faith in the household. The audience of the instruction.

keyFigures.name: Christ
keyFigures.role: Their life is hidden with him; he will appear in glory; his peace and word rule in them. The basis and goal of the instructions.

keyFigures.name: God the Father
keyFigures.role: Chooses believers, is the one whose wrath is coming (3:6), and receives thanks through Christ. The source of calling and thanksgiving.

keyFigures.name: The 'old self' and 'new self'
keyFigures.role: Put off and put on. Show the change in identity.

keyFigures.name: Greeks, Jews, barbarians, Scythians, slaves, free
keyFigures.role: Their distinctions are set aside in Christ. Show the inclusiveness of the new humanity.

keyFigures.name: Wives and husbands
keyFigures.role: Wives are to submit; husbands to love. Part of the household code.

keyFigures.name: Children and fathers
keyFigures.role: Children are to obey; fathers not to provoke. Part of the household code.

keyFigures.name: Bondservants and their masters
keyFigures.role: Bondservants are to obey sincerely and work for the Lord. Part of the household code; masters are addressed in 4:1.

keyThemes.explanation:
Because they were raised with Christ, believers are to seek the things above, and their life is hidden with Christ.

The chapter invites readers to let their identity in Christ shape their priorities.

keyThemes.theme: Putting off the old self, putting on the new
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to put to death earthly vices and put off anger and lying, and put on the new self.

The passage invites readers to see moral change as part of belonging to Christ.

keyThemes.theme: Unity in Christ across all divisions
keyThemes.explanation:
In the new self there is no Greek and Jew, slave and free; Christ is all and in all.

The chapter invites readers to see Christ as the common ground.

Believers are to put on compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forgiveness and above all love.

The passage encourages forgiving as the Lord forgave.

keyThemes.theme: Whole life lived for the Lord
keyThemes.explanation:
Word, song, thanksgiving and household relationships are to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus and as for the Lord.

Readers are invited to see ordinary relationships and work as part of serving Christ.

Colossians 4.summary: Paul tells masters to treat their bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that they also have a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1). The Colossians are to continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful with thanksgiving, and to pray also for the writers, that God may open a door for the word to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which Paul is in prison, and that he may make it clear as he ought to speak (Colossians 4:2-4). They are to walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time, with speech always gracious, seasoned with salt, so that they know how to answer each person (Colossians 4:5-6). Tychicus, a beloved brother, faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, will tell them all about Paul's activities and encourage their hearts, and with him goes Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother who is one of them (Colossians 4:7-9). Greetings come from Aristarchus, Paul's fellow prisoner; Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, whom the Colossians are to welcome if he comes; and Jesus called Justus, who are the only men of the circumcision among Paul's fellow workers for the kingdom of God and have been a comfort to him (Colossians 4:10-11). Epaphras, who is one of them, always struggles on their behalf in prayer and has worked hard for them and for those in Laodicea and Hierapolis; Luke the beloved physician and Demas also greet them (Colossians 4:12-14). The Colossians are to greet the brothers at Laodicea and Nympha and the church in her house, and when the letter has been read among them, to have it read also in the church of the Laodiceans and to read the letter from Laodicea (Colossians 4:15-16). They are to tell Archippus to fulfill the ministry he has received in the Lord (Colossians 4:17). Paul writes the final greeting with his own hand, asks them to remember his chains, and closes with 'Grace be with you' (Colossians 4:18).
Colossians 4.whereWeAre:
Paul is in prison, with fellow prisoner Aristarchus, and has an ongoing ministry through co-workers (4:3, 4:10).

Tychicus is also named as carrying Paul's letter in Ephesians 6:21-22, and Onesimus is the subject of Philemon.

Laodicea, Hierapolis and Colossae were near one another in the Lycus Valley, and Epaphras worked among all three (4:13).

Tacitus records an earthquake at Laodicea (Annals 14.27); how it affected Colossae is not stated in that passage.

Early letters were circulated among churches, as shown by the instruction to exchange letters in 4:16. The closing greetings show the web of relationships behind the letter and its delivery. They also show how Paul's co-workers served as messengers and links among churches.

keyFigures.name: Masters
keyFigures.role: Told to treat bondservants justly and fairly. They are accountable to a Master in heaven.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Asks for prayer, sends news, and sends greetings. His situation and relationships frame the closing.

keyFigures.name: Tychicus
keyFigures.role: Sent to tell the Colossians about Paul and encourage them. The messenger who carries the news.

keyFigures.name: Onesimus
keyFigures.role: Goes with Tychicus. Links Colossians with Philemon.

keyFigures.name: Aristarchus
keyFigures.role: Sends greetings. Shows Paul's companions.

keyFigures.name: Mark, the cousin of Barnabas
keyFigures.role: The Colossians are to welcome him if he comes. Shows Mark in service with Paul.

keyFigures.name: Jesus called Justus
keyFigures.role: Sends greetings. One of Paul's comforts.

keyFigures.name: Epaphras
keyFigures.role: Struggles in prayer and has worked hard for Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis. The one from whom the Colossians learned the gospel (1:7), now praying and working for the Lycus Valley churches (4:12-13).

keyFigures.name: Luke and Demas
keyFigures.role: Send greetings. Part of Paul's circle.

keyFigures.name: The Laodiceans and Nympha and the church in her house
keyFigures.role: Greeted; the letter is to be read among them. Show the connection among churches.

keyFigures.name: Archippus
keyFigures.role: Told to fulfill his ministry. Shows the church's accountability.

keyFigures.name: Outsiders
keyFigures.role: The Colossians are to walk wisely toward them. Their view matters to witness.

keyThemes.explanation:
The Colossians are to continue steadfastly in prayer with thanksgiving and to pray for Paul's ministry.

The chapter invites readers to pray steadily and watchfully.

They are to walk in wisdom toward outsiders and let speech be gracious, seasoned with salt.

The passage invites readers to consider how conduct and speech affect witness.

Masters are to treat bondservants justly and fairly, knowing they have a Master in heaven.

Readers are invited to see authority as answerable to Christ.

The chapter names many co-workers who send greetings or carry the letter.

The passage invites readers to value those who serve alongside them.

Archippus is told to fulfill his ministry, and Epaphras is described as working hard.

Readers are invited to consider their own calling.
